levels.foundation: Everyday money: saving, banking safety, inflation, scams and the very basics of investing.
levels.intermediate: How markets and products work: orders, funds, bonds, dividends, accounts and risk, at the level of an industry-essentials exam.
levels.advanced: Finance-exam-style concepts with calculations: time value of money, bond pricing and duration, valuation ratios, portfolio risk and return.

questions.question: You'll need $4,000 for a deposit on an apartment in six months. Which choice best matches that time horizon?
questions.explanation: Money needed within months should be kept safe and easy to reach, because there's no time to recover from a fall.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: Save and Invest (public domain)

questions.question: What does 'time horizon' mean in investing?
options: How long the stock market is open each day
How long until you expect to need the money
How long a company has been in business
How long it takes an order to fill
questions.explanation: Your time horizon is the period before you need the money; it shapes how much risk makes sense.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov glossary: Time Horizon (public domain)

questions.question: You deposit $1,000 at 5% interest compounded once a year. How much do you have after two years?
questions.explanation: Year one: $1,050. Year two: $1,050 x 1.05 = $1,102.50. The extra $2.50 is interest earned on interest.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: Compound Interest (public domain)

questions.question: Two friends each invest the same amount at the same rate. One starts at 25, the other at 35. Both stop at 65. Who likely ends up with more?
options: The one who started at 35, because they invest closer to retirement
They end up with the same amount
The one who started at 25, because the money compounds for longer
questions.explanation: With the same rate and amount, extra years of compounding usually make the biggest difference.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: Compound Interest (public domain)

questions.question: Why can carrying a credit card balance be so costly over time?
options: The interest compounds, so you pay interest on past interest
Credit card interest is charged only once
The bank reduces your balance each month
questions.explanation: Compounding works against you on debt: unpaid interest is added to the balance and then charged interest itself.
questions.basis: Adapted from CFPB: How does compound interest work? (public domain)

questions.question: A savings account advertises an APY. What does APY include that a simple interest rate doesn't?
options: The effect of compounding during the year
questions.explanation: Annual percentage yield shows what you'd earn in a year including compounding, so it's useful for comparing accounts.
questions.basis: FDIC Money Smart (topic: saving) (public domain)

questions.question: If inflation is 3% a year, what happens to $100 kept in a drawer?
options: It keeps exactly the same buying power
It is automatically adjusted by the bank
questions.explanation: The number stays at $100, but prices rise, so its buying power shrinks.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: What is Risk? (inflation risk) (public domain)

questions.question: What inflation rate does the US Federal Reserve aim for over the longer run?
questions.explanation: The Fed says inflation of 2% over the longer run is most consistent with its goals of maximum employment and stable prices.
questions.basis: Adapted from Federal Reserve Board FAQ (public domain)

learn_more.title: Why does the Federal Reserve aim for inflation of 2 percent over the longer run?

questions.question: What is special about US Treasury I bonds?
options: They are guaranteed to double every 5 years
They are stocks issued by the Treasury
Their interest rate includes a part linked to inflation
They are insured by the FDIC
questions.explanation: I bonds have a fixed rate plus an inflation rate that adjusts, so they help savings keep up with prices.
questions.basis: Adapted from TreasuryDirect: I bonds (public domain)

questions.question: Which is the best use of an emergency fund?
options: Buying a stock that's rising quickly
Paying for an unexpected car repair needed to get to work
A new phone because the old one is out of fashion
questions.explanation: An emergency fund is for genuine, unexpected needs, so you don't have to borrow or sell investments at a bad time.
questions.basis: FDIC Money Smart (topic: saving) (public domain)

questions.question: You want a $3,000 emergency fund within 12 months. Roughly how much should you save each month?
questions.explanation: $3,000 divided by 12 months is $250 a month.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: Savings Goal Calculator (public domain)

questions.question: What does FDIC insurance protect?
options: Your stocks if their price falls
Deposits at an insured bank if the bank fails, up to the limit
Contents of a safe deposit box
questions.explanation: FDIC insurance covers deposit accounts such as checking, savings, money market deposit accounts and CDs if an insured bank fails.
questions.basis: Adapted from FDIC: Understanding Deposit Insurance (public domain)

questions.question: Which of these is covered by FDIC insurance?
options: A certificate of deposit at an insured bank
Shares of a stock fund bought at a bank
questions.explanation: CDs at insured banks are deposits and are covered up to the limit. Investments are not, even if sold at a bank.
questions.basis: Adapted from FDIC: Are My Deposit Accounts Insured by the FDIC? (public domain)

learn_more.title: Are My Deposit Accounts Insured by the FDIC?

questions.question: Jamie has $180,000 in savings and $90,000 in checking, both in Jamie's own name at the same insured bank. How much is FDIC insured?
questions.explanation: Single accounts owned by one person at one bank are added together ($270,000) and insured up to $250,000 in total for that ownership category.
questions.basis: Adapted from FDIC: Understanding Deposit Insurance (public domain)

questions.question: Your brokerage account drops 25% because the market fell. Does SIPC cover that loss?
options: Yes, SIPC refunds market losses up to $500,000
No, SIPC does not protect against investments losing value
Only if you file a claim within a week
questions.explanation: SIPC helps when a member brokerage firm fails and customer assets are missing. It never covers ordinary market losses.
questions.basis: SIPC: What SIPC Protects

questions.question: What is a Treasury bill?
options: A short-term loan to the US government lasting a year or less
A bill you pay to the IRS
A share in the US Treasury
questions.explanation: T-bills are short-term US government securities and are considered among the safest assets.
questions.basis: Adapted from TreasuryDirect: Treasury Bills (public domain)

questions.question: What is the usual trade-off with a certificate of deposit (CD)?
options: Higher risk in exchange for unlimited withdrawals
No interest in exchange for FDIC insurance
A fixed rate in exchange for leaving the money for a set term, with a penalty for early withdrawal
A variable rate that follows the stock market
questions.explanation: CDs lock your money for a term at a set rate; taking it out early usually costs a penalty.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: Certificates of Deposit (public domain)

questions.question: How is a money market fund different from a money market deposit account at a bank?
options: The fund is an investment and isn't FDIC insured; the bank account is a deposit that is
The fund is FDIC insured; the bank account is not
The fund holds stocks; the account holds bonds
questions.explanation: Money market funds are low-risk investments but not guaranteed. Money market deposit accounts are bank deposits covered by FDIC insurance.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: Money Market Fund (public domain)

questions.question: Which statement about risk and return is generally true?
options: Higher return always means lower risk
Low-risk investments always earn the most
Investments with higher potential returns usually carry more risk
questions.explanation: Investors generally demand higher potential returns to accept more risk.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: What is Risk? (public domain)

questions.question: What does risk tolerance describe?
options: The maximum a stock can fall in a day
A rule that limits how much you can invest
How much ups and downs you can handle without abandoning your plan
The interest rate on a savings account
questions.explanation: Risk tolerance is your ability and willingness to accept swings in value.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov glossary: Risk Tolerance (public domain)

questions.question: What do you own when you buy a share of stock?
options: A small piece of ownership in the company
A promise of repayment on a set date
questions.explanation: A share is ownership. A loan to a company with repayment on a set date is a bond.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: Stocks - FAQs (public domain)

questions.question: You buy 10 shares at $30 and later sell them at $36. Ignoring fees, what's your gain?
questions.explanation: You gained $6 per share on 10 shares: 10 x $6 = $60.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: Stocks - FAQs (public domain)

questions.question: You want to buy a stock right away and don't mind small differences in price. Which order fits?
options: A limit order far below today's price
No order; shares are bought automatically
questions.explanation: A market order executes promptly at the best available price, though the exact price isn't guaranteed.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: Types of Orders (public domain)

questions.question: What does a stock market index such as the S&P 500 do?
options: Tracks the combined performance of a group of stocks
Sets the price of every stock
Lists only the stocks that went up today
questions.explanation: An index measures how a basket of stocks is doing, giving a quick read on part of the market.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov glossary: Market Index (public domain)

questions.question: What is a bear market commonly understood to mean?
options: A period when prices fall about 20% or more from a recent high
A period of steady, rising prices
questions.explanation: Bear market is an informal term for a prolonged decline, often defined as 20% or more from a recent high.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov glossary: Bear Market (public domain)

questions.question: Why do many beginners start with broad index funds?
options: They offer instant diversification at low cost
questions.explanation: A broad index fund spreads money across many companies cheaply, but it still rises and falls with the market.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov glossary: Index Fund (public domain)

questions.question: A fund charges a 0.5% expense ratio. How much does that cost per year on $4,000?
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov glossary: Expense Ratio (public domain)

questions.question: What is the main goal of diversification?
options: To own only the best stock
To reduce the damage any single investment can do
questions.explanation: Spreading money across many investments lowers the impact of any one failure. It doesn't remove all risk.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: Asset Allocation and Diversification (public domain)

questions.question: What is a dividend?
options: A payment a company makes to its shareholders, usually from profits
A fee you pay to buy shares
Interest paid on a savings account
questions.explanation: Dividends distribute part of a company's earnings to shareholders. They're not guaranteed.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov glossary: Dividend (public domain)

questions.question: Which is an example of dollar-cost averaging?
options: Investing only when the news is good
Investing a random amount whenever you feel like it
Investing $150 into the same fund every month
questions.explanation: Dollar-cost averaging means investing a fixed amount on a regular schedule, regardless of price.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov glossary: Dollar Cost Averaging (public domain)

questions.question: The market falls 15% in a month and you feel like selling everything. According to this course, what's the main risk of acting on that feeling?
options: Locking in losses and missing a possible recovery
questions.explanation: Panic selling turns temporary declines into permanent losses and can mean missing the rebound.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: What is Risk? (public domain)

questions.question: A caller promises 'guaranteed 30% returns with no risk' if you invest today. What should you do?
options: Treat it as a red flag, take time and check the seller's registration
Invest quickly before the offer expires
Send a small amount by gift card to test it
questions.explanation: Guaranteed high returns and pressure to hurry are classic signs of fraud. Checking registration is a good first step.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: How to Avoid Fraud (public domain)

questions.question: How does a Ponzi scheme pay its early investors?
options: With money from newer investors, not real profits
questions.explanation: Ponzi schemes collapse when new money dries up, because there are no real earnings behind the payouts.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: Ponzi Scheme (public domain)

questions.question: Your employer adds 50 cents to your 401(k) for every $1 you contribute, up to 6% of pay. You earn $40,000 and contribute 6%. How much does the employer add?
questions.explanation: 6% of $40,000 is $2,400 from you. Half of that, $1,200, comes from the employer match.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov glossary: 401(k) Plan (public domain)

questions.question: When do you generally owe US tax on a capital gain from a stock in a regular brokerage account?
options: When you sell the stock for more than you paid
questions.explanation: Gains are generally taxed when realised, meaning when you sell.
questions.basis: Adapted from IRS Topic no. 409 (public domain)

learn_more.title: Topic no. 409, Capital gains and losses

questions.question: A company sells new shares to investors for the first time in an IPO. Where does that sale take place?
questions.explanation: New securities sold by the issuer are sold in the primary market; later trading between investors is the secondary market.
questions.basis: FINRA SIE outline: Knowledge of Capital Markets

questions.question: Compared with common stock, preferred stock typically...
options: Usually pays a fixed dividend and ranks ahead of common stock for dividends and in liquidation, but usually has no vote
Has more votes and no dividends
Is a type of bond insured by the FDIC
questions.explanation: Preferred shareholders usually get priority on dividends and in liquidation, in exchange for limited voting rights and upside.
questions.basis: FINRA SIE outline: Understanding Products and Their Risks (equity securities)

questions.question: You own 100 shares at $80. The company does a 2-for-1 stock split. What do you own afterwards, before any price change?
questions.explanation: A split changes the number of shares and the price per share, not the total value: still $8,000.
questions.basis: FINRA SIE outline: Understanding Products and Their Risks (corporate actions)

questions.question: A stock's bid is $25.40 and ask is $25.45. You buy 200 shares with a market order and immediately sell them with a market order. Ignoring commissions and price changes, what does the round trip cost?
questions.explanation: You buy near the ask and sell near the bid, losing the $0.05 spread on 200 shares: 200 x $0.05 = $10.
questions.basis: FINRA SIE outline: Trading, Customer Accounts and Prohibited Activities (orders and quotes)

questions.question: A stock trades at $50. You place a sell stop order at $45. What happens if the price drops to $45?
options: The order becomes a market order and sells at the next available price, which may be below $45
questions.explanation: Once the stop price is reached, a stop order becomes a market order, so the fill price isn't guaranteed in a fast-moving market.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: Types of Orders (public domain)

questions.question: You place a limit order to buy at $30 when a stock trades at $32. What's true?
options: It fills at $30 even if the price rises
It fills only if the stock can be bought at $30 or less
questions.explanation: A buy limit order sets the maximum price you'll pay; it may never fill.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov glossary: Limit Orders (public domain)

questions.question: What role does a market maker play?
options: Sets the official price of every stock
Stands ready to buy and sell a stock, posting bid and ask quotes
Regulates brokers on behalf of the SEC
questions.explanation: Market makers provide liquidity by quoting both sides and typically earn the spread.
questions.basis: FINRA SIE outline: Knowledge of Capital Markets (market structure)

questions.question: For most US stock trades, settlement now happens one business day after the trade (T+1). What does settlement mean?
options: The trade is reported in the news
Cash and shares officially change hands
questions.explanation: The trade date is when you agree to buy or sell; settlement is when ownership and payment are formally exchanged.
questions.basis: FINRA SIE outline: Trading, Customer Accounts and Prohibited Activities (settlement)

questions.question: An index weighted by market capitalisation is most affected by which companies?
options: Those with the highest share price
The largest companies by total market value
questions.explanation: In a cap-weighted index such as the S&P 500, bigger companies carry bigger weights. The Dow, by contrast, is price-weighted.
questions.basis: FINRA SIE outline: Knowledge of Capital Markets (indexes)

questions.question: When interest rates rise, why might stock prices fall even if company profits don't change?
options: Future profits are worth less in today's money and safer assets pay more
Companies are banned from paying dividends
Rising rates always cause recessions immediately
Stocks pay interest that falls when rates rise
questions.explanation: A higher discount rate lowers the present value of future cash flows, and bonds and savings become stiffer competition.
questions.basis: FINRA SIE outline: Understanding Products and Their Risks (market risk)

questions.question: The VIX rises sharply from 15 to 35. What is it signalling?
options: Investors expect much larger S&P 500 swings over the next 30 days
questions.explanation: The VIX reflects expected volatility from option prices. It says nothing about direction.
questions.basis: FINRA SIE outline: Understanding Products and Their Risks (options and volatility)

questions.question: When you place an order to buy a traditional mutual fund during the trading day, what price do you usually get?
options: The price at the moment you click buy
The fund's net asset value calculated after that day's close
questions.explanation: Mutual fund orders are filled at the next calculated NAV, usually after the market closes. ETFs trade at market prices during the day.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: Mutual Funds (public domain)

questions.question: A fund holds $105 million of assets, owes $5 million and has 4 million shares outstanding. What is its NAV per share?
questions.explanation: NAV = (assets - liabilities) / shares = ($105m - $5m) / 4m = $25.00.
questions.basis: FINRA SIE outline: Understanding Products and Their Risks (investment companies)

questions.question: Two index funds track the same index. Fund A charges 0.04% and Fund B charges 0.60%. Over the long run, what's the most likely result before taxes?
options: Fund B returns more because it charges more
Fund A returns more, by roughly the fee difference each year
Fund A must hold riskier stocks
questions.explanation: Funds tracking the same index hold nearly the same investments, so the cost difference flows almost directly to returns.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov glossary: Expense Ratio (public domain)

questions.question: A $1,000 bond pays a 4% annual coupon. How much interest does it pay each year?
questions.explanation: Coupon payments are based on face value: 4% x $1,000 = $40 a year.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov glossary: Coupon (public domain)

questions.question: A 26-week Treasury bill with $1,000 face value is bought for $980. How do you earn interest?
options: You receive $980 back plus a dividend
Interest is paid only if rates rise
You receive $1,000 at maturity; the $20 difference is your interest
questions.explanation: T-bills are typically sold at a discount and repaid at face value; the difference is the interest.
questions.basis: Adapted from TreasuryDirect: Treasury Bills (public domain)

questions.question: Which bond rating is the lowest that is still considered 'investment grade' by S&P?
questions.explanation: S&P ratings from BBB- upward are investment grade; BB+ and below are high-yield (junk).
questions.basis: FINRA SIE outline: Understanding Products and Their Risks (debt securities)

questions.question: Why might a company call (repay early) its bonds?
options: Interest rates have fallen, so it can borrow again more cheaply
questions.explanation: Issuers tend to call bonds when rates fall, which leaves investors reinvesting at lower rates (reinvestment risk).
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: Bonds - FAQs (public domain)

questions.question: What is a common tax feature of US municipal bonds?
options: They are always exempt from every tax
They are taxed at double the normal rate
Their interest is generally exempt from federal income tax
questions.explanation: Muni bond interest is generally federally tax-exempt and may also be exempt from state tax for in-state residents. Capital gains can still be taxed.
questions.basis: FINRA SIE outline: Understanding Products and Their Risks (municipal securities)

questions.question: What happens to the principal of a Treasury Inflation-Protected Security (TIPS) when inflation rises?
questions.explanation: TIPS principal rises with inflation and falls with deflation; at maturity you get the adjusted or original principal, whichever is greater.
questions.basis: Adapted from TreasuryDirect: TIPS (public domain)

questions.question: Which risk is the main concern for someone holding a long-term bond paying a fixed 3% while inflation runs at 5%?
options: Business risk of a single company
questions.explanation: Fixed payments buy less when inflation exceeds the coupon, eroding real returns.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: What is Risk? (public domain)

questions.question: What is liquidity risk?
options: The risk that interest rates rise
The risk of a company failing
The risk you can't sell quickly without accepting a much lower price
questions.explanation: Thinly traded assets can be hard to sell at a fair price when you need to.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: What is Risk? (public domain)

questions.question: Your target is 60% stocks and 40% bonds. After a strong year you're at 70/30. What does rebalancing involve?
options: Buying more stocks because they did well
Selling some stocks and buying bonds to return to 60/40
questions.explanation: Rebalancing restores your chosen risk level by trimming what grew and adding to what lagged.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov glossary: Rebalancing (public domain)

questions.question: A stock pays a quarterly dividend of $0.75 and trades at $60. What is its annual dividend yield?
questions.explanation: Annual dividend = 4 x $0.75 = $3.00. Yield = $3.00 / $60 = 5.0%.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov glossary: Dividend (public domain)

questions.question: To receive an upcoming dividend, when must you generally buy the stock?
options: On or after the ex-dividend date
Any time before the year ends
questions.explanation: Buyers on or after the ex-dividend date don't get that dividend; the seller does.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov glossary: Dividend (public domain)

questions.question: Which SEC filing contains a US public company's quarterly financial statements?
questions.explanation: The 10-Q is the quarterly report; the 10-K is the more detailed annual report.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov glossary: Form 10-Q (public domain)

questions.question: You buy $10,000 of stock using $5,000 of your own money and $5,000 borrowed on margin. The stock falls 20%. Ignoring interest, what happens to your own money?
options: Nothing, the broker absorbs the loss
questions.explanation: The holding drops $2,000 to $8,000, but you still owe $5,000. Your equity is $3,000: a 40% loss. Leverage magnifies losses.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov glossary: Margin Account (public domain)

questions.question: What is the maximum possible loss when you short-sell a stock?
options: The amount you received when you sold
In theory, unlimited, because the price can keep rising
questions.explanation: A short seller must buy the shares back later. There's no ceiling on how high the price can go.
questions.basis: FINRA SIE outline: Trading, Customer Accounts and Prohibited Activities (short sales)

questions.question: Promoters buy a thinly traded stock, spread false hype online, then sell as others pile in. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Pump-and-dump schemes are illegal manipulation that leave late buyers holding shares at collapsed prices.
questions.basis: Adapted from SEC Investor.gov: Pump and Dump Schemes (public domain)

questions.question: What is the key tax difference between a traditional IRA and a Roth IRA?
options: Traditional may give a deduction now and is taxed on withdrawal; Roth uses after-tax money and qualified withdrawals are tax-free
questions.explanation: The difference is when you pay tax: later for traditional, up front for Roth.
questions.basis: Adapted from IRS: Traditional and Roth IRAs (public domain)

questions.topic: Time value of money: future value
questions.question: $5,000 is invested at 6% compounded annually for 10 years. What is the future value (to the nearest dollar)?
questions.explanation: FV = 5,000 x 1.06^10 = 5,000 x 1.7908 = about $8,954. $8,000 is what simple (non-compounded) interest would give.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Quantitative Methods (time value of money)

questions.topic: Time value of money: present value
questions.question: How much must you invest today at 8% compounded annually to have $10,000 in five years (to the nearest dollar)?
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Quantitative Methods (time value of money)

questions.question: You invest $1,000 at the end of each year for three years at 10% a year. What is the total value right after the third deposit?
questions.explanation: First deposit grows two years ($1,210), second grows one year ($1,100), third has no growth ($1,000): $3,310 in total.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Quantitative Methods (annuities)

questions.question: A loan charges 12% a year compounded monthly. What is the effective annual rate (to two decimals)?
questions.explanation: EAR = (1 + 0.12/12)^12 - 1 = 1.01^12 - 1 = 12.68%. Compounding more often raises the effective rate.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Quantitative Methods (interest rates)

questions.question: At 9% a year, the Rule of 72 estimates 8 years to double. What is the exact doubling time (to one decimal)?
questions.explanation: Exact time = ln(2) / ln(1.09) = 0.6931 / 0.0862 = about 8.04 years, so the rule is very close at this rate.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Quantitative Methods (time value of money)

questions.question: An investment returns 8% in a year when inflation is 3%. What is the exact real return (to two decimals)?
questions.explanation: Real return = (1.08 / 1.03) - 1 = 4.85%. Subtracting (8% - 3% = 5%) is only an approximation.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Quantitative Methods / Economics (nominal vs real rates)

questions.question: At 3% annual inflation, roughly what will $100,000 in 25 years be worth in today's money?
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Quantitative Methods (time value of money)

learn_more.title: Why does the Federal Reserve aim for inflation of 2 percent over the longer run?

questions.question: An investment gains 50% one year and loses 50% the next. What is its compound (geometric) average annual return?
questions.explanation: $100 becomes $150, then $75. Geometric average = sqrt(0.75) - 1 = -13.4%. The arithmetic average of 0% overstates the result.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Quantitative Methods (rates and returns)

questions.question: You buy a stock at $50, receive $2 in dividends and sell it a year later at $54. What is your holding period return?
questions.explanation: HPR = (price change + income) / start price = ($4 + $2) / $50 = 12%.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Quantitative Methods (rates and returns)

questions.question: A 2-year bond has a $1,000 face value and pays a 5% annual coupon. If market yields are 6%, what is its price (to the nearest dollar)?
questions.explanation: Price = 50/1.06 + 1,050/1.06^2 = 47.17 + 934.50 = $981.67. It trades below par because its coupon is below the market yield.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Fixed Income (bond valuation)

questions.question: A bond's coupon rate is 6% and its yield to maturity is 4%. How is it priced?
questions.explanation: When the coupon exceeds the market yield, buyers pay more than face value; the premium shrinks toward par at maturity.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Fixed Income (bond valuation)

questions.question: A $1,000 face value bond pays a 4% coupon and trades at $800. What is its current yield?
questions.explanation: Current yield = annual coupon / price = $40 / $800 = 5.0%.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Fixed Income (yield measures)

questions.question: A bond has a modified duration of 7. If its yield rises by 1 percentage point, roughly how does its price change?
questions.explanation: Approximate price change = -duration x change in yield = -7 x 1% = -7%. (Convexity makes the actual drop slightly smaller.)
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Fixed Income (interest rate risk and duration)

questions.question: Which of these 10-year bonds has the highest interest-rate sensitivity (duration)?
options: All three have the same duration
questions.explanation: With no coupons, all the cash comes at maturity, so the zero has the longest duration of the three.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Fixed Income (interest rate risk and duration)

questions.question: A company earns net income of $240 million, pays $40 million in preferred dividends and has 50 million common shares. What is its basic EPS?
questions.explanation: Basic EPS = (net income - preferred dividends) / common shares = $200m / 50m = $4.00.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Financial Statement Analysis (income statements and EPS)

questions.question: A stock trades at $45 with EPS of $3. What are its P/E ratio and earnings yield?
questions.explanation: P/E = $45 / $3 = 15. Earnings yield is the inverse: $3 / $45 = about 6.7%.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Equity Investments (price multiples)

questions.question: A company has a market cap of $30 billion and net income of $1.5 billion. What is its P/E ratio?
questions.explanation: P/E can be computed at the company level: market cap / net income = $30bn / $1.5bn = 20.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Equity Investments (price multiples)

questions.question: A stock is expected to pay a $2 dividend next year, growing 3% a year forever. Investors require 8%. Using the constant-growth model, what is its value?
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Equity Investments (equity valuation)

questions.question: A portfolio is 60% in stocks expected to return 8% and 40% in bonds expected to return 3%. What is its expected return?
questions.explanation: Expected return is the weighted average: 0.6 x 8% + 0.4 x 3% = 4.8% + 1.2% = 6.0%.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Portfolio Management (portfolio risk and return)

questions.question: Two assets each have volatility of 20%. A 50/50 portfolio of them would have the LOWEST volatility when their correlation is...
questions.explanation: The lower the correlation, the more the assets offset each other. At -1, a 50/50 mix of equally volatile assets would have zero volatility in theory.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Portfolio Management (diversification and correlation)

questions.question: Asset X has 20% volatility and asset Y has 10%. Their correlation is 0. What is the volatility of a 50/50 portfolio (to one decimal)?
questions.explanation: Variance = 0.5^2 x 0.20^2 + 0.5^2 x 0.10^2 = 0.0100 + 0.0025 = 0.0125. Volatility = sqrt(0.0125) = 11.2%, less than the 15% weighted average.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Portfolio Management (portfolio risk and return)

questions.question: Which risk remains even in a portfolio holding thousands of stocks?
options: The risk of one CEO resigning
The risk of one product recall
questions.explanation: Diversification removes most company-specific (unsystematic) risk, but economy-wide shocks affect nearly all stocks.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Portfolio Management (systematic and unsystematic risk)

questions.question: The risk-free rate is 3%, the expected market return is 8% and a stock's beta is 1.2. What is its expected return under CAPM?
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Portfolio Management (CAPM)

questions.question: A fund returns 9% a year with 15% volatility. The risk-free rate is 3%. What is its Sharpe ratio?
questions.explanation: Sharpe ratio = (return - risk-free rate) / volatility = (9% - 3%) / 15% = 0.40.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Portfolio Management (risk-adjusted return)

questions.question: $100,000 is invested for 20 years. One option nets 6% a year; another nets 5% because of a 1% higher fee. How much more does the cheaper option end with (nearest $1,000)?
questions.explanation: 100,000 x 1.06^20 = $320,714 versus 100,000 x 1.05^20 = $265,330: a gap of about $55,384, more than half the original investment.
questions.basis: CFA Level I topic: Portfolio Management (investment costs)
